candidate_sentences.text: On November 13, 2025, a disturbance occurred when a planned outage of a 500 kV transmission line resulted in uncontrolled, widespread outages across the northeastern region of the Western Interconnection (WI).
To understand the underlying causes and contributing factors, WECC and NERC partnered with the stakeholders involved to conduct a comprehensive analysis.
This report contains details of the disturbance, the contributing factors identified through the analysis, and the resulting considerations.
One of the primary goals of the reliable operation8 of the Bulk Electric System (BES)9 is preventing cascading outages.
To achieve this goal, operation of the BES is conducted in a coordinated manner.
NERC defines cascading as “The uncontrolled successive loss of System Elements triggered by an incident at any location.

Cascading results in widespread electric service interruption that cannot be restrained from sequentially spreading beyond an area predetermined by studies.” System Overview Wyoming produces about 12 times more energy than it consumes.
This excess energy is transmitted through an extensive network of long, high-voltage transmission lines to load centers throughout the WI.
To aid in transmission of this generation, PacifiCorp East (PACE) built its Energy Gateway project10.
As part of this project, the Aeolus–Anticline line was placed in service in 2020 and the Aeolus–Clover line in 2024.
The WI has four Reliability Coordinators (RC) who oversee and coordinate the operations of the BES.
Part of their responsibility is to coordinate and monitor equipment outages to ensure no combination of outages has an adverse effect on the reliable operation of their respective areas.
In this region, the RC oversight is split between RC West (RCW) and SPP West (SPP), as illustrated in Figure 1, establishing an RC seam11.
This event occurred in November, a shoulder month, when a significant amount of maintenance is performed on BES lines and equipment.

Operating the elements of the BPS within equipment and electric system thermal, voltage, and stability limits so instability, uncontrolled separation, or cascading failures of the system will not occur as a result of a sudden disturbance, including a cybersecurity incident or unanticipated failure of system elements.
Transmission elements operated at 100 kV or higher and real power and reactive power resources connected at 100 kV or higher.
This does not include facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.

Energy Gateway , PacifiCorp.com The operational, administrative, or physical boundaries between two or more RCs, or between different market areas, designed to ensure the reliable operation of the BES.

As the "highest level of authority" for grid operations, RCs are responsible for maintaining stability across their respective areas, and "seams" are the critical interfaces where these entities must coordinate to prevent congestion, manage loop flows, and maintain reliability.
Figure 1: WI RC Areas Entities are responsible for scheduling outages to repair and maintain their BES equipment, prioritizing these activities, and submitting planned outages to their RCs.
The RC conducts a feasibility assessment of the submitted outages to ensure there are no adverse effects on the system.

If potential impacts are identified, they coordinate with the entity — and neighboring RCs when necessary — to develop appropriate mitigation plans, including adjusting the outage schedule by shifting dates or times or rescheduling the outage entirely.
Pre-Disturbance Conditions On November 12, 2025, the day before the disturbance, several transmission lines in this region were already out of service for maintenance, as shown in Figure 2.
The lines included: • Mustang–Spence 230 kV line • Laramie River–Dave Johnston 230 kV line • Yellowtail–Sheridan 230 kV line • Teckla–Osage 230 kV line • Platte–Standpipe 230 kV line

• Jim Bridger–Mustang 230 kV line • Crossover–Yellowtail 230 kV line • Rapid City DC tie Figure 2: Status of facilities before planned switching (out-of-service facilities marked with X) The OPAs performed by RCW, SPP, and PACE did not indicate any reliability issues for the outage of the Aeolus–Clover line, which was scheduled to occur from 0800 to 0900 hrs.12 (See Appendix A — OPA for additional information).
The Aeolus–Clover line outage was planned to facilitate the return to service of Little Snake Reactor #1 and to remove Coyote Reactor #2 from service.
The Little Snake reactor had been out of service since November 8 and was scheduled back in service at noon.
Following the switching of the reactors, the Aeolus–Clover line would be returned to service, and the Coyote Reactor #2 would remain out of service with a scheduled return on November 19, 2025.
The PACE Grid Operator East (GOE) started switching for the outage of the Aeolus–Clover line at 0800 hrs., effectively bypassing the series capacitors at Coyote substation.
Soon after, the PACE GOE was notified of a delay in personnel arriving at the Little Snake substation.
Switching personnel were not scheduled to be at Little Snake substation until later due to the scheduled noon end time of the outage of Little Snake Reactor #1.
The PACE GOE notified RCW of the delay in switching with a new projected start time of noon.
Due to the delay in the line switching, the PACE GOE re-inserted the series capacitors at Coyote substation.
Meanwhile, WACM proceeded with the scheduled outage of the Miracle Mile West main bus for periodic maintenance (scheduled from 0900 to 1700 hrs.).

SPP identified in its Real-time Assessment (RTA)13 studies that the simultaneous outages of the Aeolus–Clover line and the Miracle Mile West main bus would require mitigation plans to maintain the reliable operation of the BES.
SPP informed WACM that there was not a good mitigation plan to support overlapping the outage of their Miracle Mile West main bus and PACE Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line.
SPP also informed RCW that studies with the overlapping outages showed overloads up to 130% on the remaining Alcova–Miracle Mile East 115 kV line, even with assuming activation of the Aeolus RAS.

Due to these study results involving outages across the RC seam, SPP would not allow the outages to overlap and notified WACM that it could not proceed with the Miracle Mile outage until the Aeolus–Clover line was returned to service.

RCW notified SPP that the Aeolus–Clover line outage was delayed for 3 hours due to the absence of a switching personnel scheduled at Little Snake until noon, when the line was originally planned to be returned to service.
RCW also indicated that if WACM would like to proceed with its Miracle Mile West main bus outage, PACE agreed to limit its wind as needed to mitigate any overloads.
Subsequently, SPP approved WACM to move forward with its outage.
WACM proceeded to switch the Miracle Mile West main bus at 0950 hrs. with a scheduled return time of 1700 hrs. and included the Alcova–Miracle Mile West 115 kV line.
During the outage, as anticipated, increased loading was observed on the remaining Alcova–Miracle Mile East line.
In response, SPP requested system adjustments such as phase shifters in a neighboring utility to help mitigate the increased loading.

As the area generation increased, and the start time of the PACE Aeolus–Clover line outage approached, the RCs and utilities studied what system adjustments would be needed to accommodate both outages.
SPPs studies showed loading of 138% on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line for loss of the PACE Aeolus–Anticline line.

SPP and WACM agreed they would perform a study to identify An evaluation of system conditions using real-time data to assess existing (pre-contingency) and potential (post-contingency) operating conditions.
potential PACE wind reductions if both the Aeolus–Clover line and the Miracle Mile bus outages occurred simultaneously.
Their study identified that about 400 MW of wind reduction would be needed to mitigate the loading on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line.
SPP and WACM discussed current system outages and potential mitigation measures such as adjusting phase shifters to provide relief.

WACM studies showed that if the Aeolus–Clover line was removed from service, the loading would increase to over 130% with the next contingent loss of the Dave Johnston–Goshen 230 kV line, even with the 400 MW of previously identified wind reductions.

SPP informed RCW of significant reliability concerns on the WACM Alcova–Miracle Mile East line loading if overlapped with the PACE outage, and use of area phase-shifters would not be enough to mitigate the exceedances.
Studies conducted by SPP, RCW, and WACM all indicated the need for additional reductions to PACE wind generation in the area.
RCW’s analysis showed that approximately 820 MW of wind would need to be reduced, bringing output down to about 2,500 MW, to support both outages.
The RCs discussed relaying this information to PACE to determine whether it would begin reducing wind generation before the planned 500 kV line outage.

RCW discussed with PACE the possibility of overlapping the outages with WACM and stated that its studies indicated a need for a wind-generation reduction of 820 MW from the current 3,300 MW level, including the specific locations where generation was reduced in the analysis.
PACE acknowledged the information and stated it was awaiting study results from WACM, after which it would begin the required work.
SPP later informed RCW that WACM was evaluating the proposed 820 MW PACE wind reduction.
RCW notified PACE that it was seeing loading over 125% on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line for loss of the Aeolus–Clover line and asked whether PACE could complete its wind reduction.

PACE was delaying the wind reduction due to a massive telecommunications outage that was affecting its ability to raise generation outside the Wyoming area to compensate for the reduction of wind generation.
As RC and PACE were looking into solutions, such as manual reductions, WACM encountered some equipment issues and made the decision to return the Miracle Mile bus back to service.
Returning this equipment would resolve most of the overload concerns.
At this time RCW and PACE agreed to a 200 MW reduction in wind generation.
WACM notified SPP that the Miracle Mile bus had returned to service at 1156 hrs.
SPP notified RCW that the return of the bus had improved their contingency analysis.
RCW confirmed that PACE still wanted to take the Aeolus–Clover line outage and that it was seeing no issues with taking the outage.
RCW notified PACE that the Miracle Mile bus had returned to service and that PACE could hold off on the wind reductions currently in progress.
PACE confirmed this and conveyed that it had a big
communications outage that was affecting its state estimator14 in the southern Utah area.
PACE stated that it would monitor the Hosted Advanced Network Application15 tool provided by RCW.
Due to the communications outage, the PACE shift supervisor took over switching from the PACE GOE.
Aeolus RAS Protocol In preparation for the Aeolus–Clover line outage, PACE raised the Aeolus RAS arming setpoints above the current actual flow16.
This effectively disarmed the RAS for the current conditions and prevented any trips from being sent to generation facilities if a monitored piece of equipment tripped or was taken out of service.
PACE performed contingency analysis with the RAS setpoints adjusted in this manner to identify any issues.
Typically, when issues are revealed in post-contingency analysis, PACE will reduce generation in the study until the issues are cleared.
PACE would then use the amount of generation reduced in the contingency analysis as the amount of generation reduction needed before switching.
In this instance, it identified no issues in the contingency analysis, and so took no reductions in the wind, and the RAS was left in this adjusted status.
Impacts on RCW, SPP, and PACE resulting from adjusting the Aeolus RAS setpoints are covered in the following paragraphs.

RCW The next real-time contingency analysis (RTCA) scan, after the Aeolus RAS setpoints were adjusted to enable switching, started showing low voltage results, specifically in the Aeolus and Anticline areas.
The RTCA identified low voltage results for the loss of the Aeolus–Clover line with up to 120% exceedance of the Low Emergency rating at the Anticline 500 kV bus.
RCW noticed there was no generation dropping due to Aeolus RAS operation in its RTCA solutions, but, at that time, RCW had no reason to believe the RAS was not armed.
RCW has a data historian display with white boxes to indicate RAS status.
The box changes from solid to empty on arming changes, making it difficult to notice when these changes occur.
There are no alarms associated with this change to help RC awareness of the RAS arming status.

In addition: • There were no notes indicating the RAS setpoints would be adjusted for this outage. • There was no phone call from PACE providing verbal notification that the RAS setpoints had been adjusted.
Computes the best estimate of a grid's voltage magnitudes and angles using redundant and scattered measurements; e.g., SCADA/PMU.
It transforms raw data into a reliable, real-time snapshot of the network, enabling security monitoring, bad data detection, and contingency analysis.

Used to perform RTCA, as a "hosted" application from RCW, allowing smaller BAs and TOPs to use the centralized, high-performance computing infrastructure of a major RC to run their own localized studies.
This RAS setpoint adjustment was consistent with PacifiCorp's RAS Operating Manual.
• There was no energy management system (EMS)17 alarm available to indicate the RAS setpoints had been adjusted by raising the arming limit.
In addition to this RAS visibility issue, there had been approximately 64 instances of unsolved RTCA contingencies18 in this area in the previous two months with corresponding RTCA violation alarms.
Offline studies during these instances were able to be resolved, indicating no system reliability issues.

This history of unsolved indications, along with lack of RAS visibility, reduced RCW’s confidence that the results it was seeing before the scheduled outage were valid, preventing it from recognizing the N-1 insecure state and directing PACE to hold off on the switching.
RCW asked its operating engineer (OE) to perform an off-line study to confirm the RTCA results.
The OE could get the studies to solve but was not satisfied with the results and would investigate further.
At 1220 hrs., RCW called PACE to discuss “a couple things.” RCW asked about the communications outage in southern Utah and whether PACE still planned to take the outage.
PACE reported the estimated time for repairs of the communications outage was 3 hours at least due to the site location.
In response, RCW asked whether the outage would be delayed “until the comms stuff” was figured out.

PACE responded that it still planned to take the Aeolus–Clover line out soon, noting that the communications outage should not affect the outage “since [PacifiCorp did not] need to move generation around so much.” Before the call ended, PACE agreed to provide updates on the “comms stuff.” This was not intended as a go-ahead from RCW for the Aeolus–Clover outage.
RCW anticipated a reduction in wind generation before the line was switched out of service.

PACE’s understanding from a previous conversation (on the wind reduction no longer being needed for overloads seen with the Miracle Mile bus outage) was that, with the bus returned to service, no wind reduction was needed for the Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line outage.
In the next RTCA scan, RCW showed the Aeolus–Clover contingency was converging.
Other unsolved contingencies in the region were the Anticline 500 kV transformer, Anticline–Jim Bridger 345 kV line, and the Aeolus–Anticline line.

RCW’s last scan before the event showed unsolved contingencies in the area for the Aeolus–Clover line, Anticline 500–345 kV transformer, Anticline–Jim Bridger 345 kV line, and the Aeolus–Anticline line.
With different understandings of when the outage would begin, no further communication occurred between RCW and PACE before the outage.
SPP SPP confirmed it was showing clear contingency results due to the return of the Miracle Mile bus.
The Aeolus–Clover line is in the RCW area.

SPP does include areas outside of its RC area in its studies, but For power systems, this is a software-driven platform that monitors, controls, and optimizes electrical grid performance, generation, and storage.
An unsolved contingency in RTCA occurs when the system software cannot calculate a stable post-contingency state for a specific component failure (such as a line or generator trip).
This often indicates a potential voltage collapse, instability, or a highly infeasible operating state.
because they are outside of its area of responsibility, those areas may not have the same level of alarms or visibility.

For the Aeolus area, which is outside its RC area, SPP models the RAS in its RTCA but has no visibility of the RAS’s arming status and assumes the RAS is available in its studies unless notified by RCW.

With no notification of a change in RAS arming status, before the event, SPP’s RTCA study showed no contingency issues of concern and solved with the Aeolus RAS tripping an appropriate amount of generation, making SPP unaware of the actual N-1 insecure state caused by the setpoints for the Aeolus RAS having been adjusted for the line outage.
PACE Adjusting the setpoints for the Aeolus RAS allowed RTCA to provide results that were not masked by RAS actions.
The PACE RTCA performed several runs with no contingencies identified that would prevent it from removing the Aeolus–Clover line from service.
Due to issues with RTCA alarming thresholds that were not understood at the time of the event, PACE was unaware that the system had entered an N-1 insecure state.
After the event, and looking closer at the solution, PACE discovered that, although its RTCA did solve, the Aeolus 500 kV bus voltage without RAS action was 450 kV.
Normally, this voltage level would indicate a violation of the low voltage limits showing an unacceptable RTCA solution.

PACE discovered that the alarming for these voltage violations had not been enabled in its RTCA system when these busses were first commissioned in 2020, preventing the alarms from indicating problems with the scheduled line outage.
Additionally, PACE determined that the voltage drop seen during the event was greater than the 450 kV in the RTCA solution.
Normally, in RTCA, as the voltage drops, the modeled generators will provide reactive current following a modeled megavolt-amperes reactive (Mvar) curve up to the identified limit.
In PACE’s RTCA, 43% of the units modeled did not have these curves or were not set to limit voltage.
This allowed these units in the model to produce Mvar beyond the physical capability of the actual units.
In essence, they would do what they needed to do to solve the case, masking the actual risk involved with the scheduled line outage.

PACE also discovered that the contingency model for the Aeolus–Clover line and several other contingencies in the area had flags set incorrectly, resulting in contingencies not being monitored and alarmed in real time as expected.
At 12:43:34, without further communication with RCW, the Aeolus–Clover line was removed from service.
PACE Event Before the planned outage of the Aeolus–Clover transmission line, there were eight other 230 kV transmission lines already out of service in the area for planned outages.
As per the switching order to de-energize the Aeolus–Clover transmission line for the planned outage, the PACE system operator opened the Aeolus 11G62 circuit breaker at 12:43:34.460.
Opening this breaker disconnected the Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line from the Aeolus 500 kV bus.
Immediately, the Aeolus 500 kV bus voltage started to decline rapidly (See Figure 3).
from ~1.0 pu to ~0.28 pu in 344 milliseconds, at which time the Aeolus–Anticline line tripped correctly on Zone 1 due to the extremely low voltage.
At the time of the Aeolus–Anticline line trip, the Windstar 230 kV bus voltage was ~0.78 pu.
When the Aeolus–Anticline line tripped, the Windstar 230 kV bus voltage decline accelerated, reaching ~0.23 pu in the next 279 milliseconds.
During this period, 13 additional 230 kV transmission lines tripped correctly on Zone 1 due to the extremely low voltage.

The single 500 kV and 13 230 kV transmission lines tripping resulted in the separation and islanding of northeast Wyoming and southwestern South Dakota from the WI 623 milliseconds after opening the Aeolus–Clover line.

Table 1: Line loss sequence of events Facility Outage Time Cause The rapid decline of voltage after opening the Aeolus–Clover line was due to a lack of adequate reactive power to maintain voltage for the magnitude of power flow through the transmission topology that existed after opening the line.
The resulting electrical island formed and collapsed within 6 seconds from the initial event.
The system disturbance resulted in high system frequency measured at Dave Johnston up to 62.76 Hz at 12:43:35 subsequently tripping Dave Johnston units #1–4 on over frequency.
Units #1 and #2 performed a whole unit trip (G lockout) at 12:43:34 and 12:43:36 respectively.
Unit #3 performed a prime mover trip at 12:43:35 followed by the whole unit trip on (U lockout) due to an exciter trip at 12:46:28.
Dave Johnston Unit #4 performed a prime mover trip (S lockout) at 12:43:35.
This unit’s protection also includes a reverse-power relay designed to prevent the generator from motoring by detecting and isolating the unit if power begins flowing into it from the grid.

The Dave Johnston 230 kV bus was initially de-energized and was later re-energized at a voltage below the reverse power detection threshold, so the Unit #4 reverse-power relays did not operate, leaving the generator electrically connected to the grid and preventing a whole unit trip.
Figure 3: Aeolus 500 kV bus volts (orange marks the time of Aeolus–Clover line opening; magenta marks the time of Aeolus–Anticline tripping).
The magnitude of the generation loss was ~120% of the WI’s Resource Loss Protection Criteria (RLPC).

While the frequency nadir was exceptionally low, because of the magnitude of the loss and the relatively low inertia and demand on the interconnection, performance was exceptional and margin to the WI underfrequency load shedding was greater than .25 Hz.

Additionally, the initial frequency recovery immediately before any deployment of contingency reserves indicates primary frequency response, measured at the A-B space, was -2,840 MW/.10 Hz, double the Interconnection Frequency Response Obligation of -1,420 MW/.10 Hz19.
This exceptional performance is believed to be a result of the resource mix online at the time of the event.

As a result of this cascading outage, impacts in PACE, Black Hills Energy (BHE), Tri-State G&T (TSGT), WACM, and Montana–Alberta Tie Line (MATL) included generation, transmission equipment, load, and customer loss.
In total, within 6 seconds, 33 BES transmission lines, approximately 1,120 MW load, approximately 4,853 MW of generation, and service to over 250,000 customers were lost.
In response to the large amount of generation lost, several members of the Northwest Power Pool (NWPP) Reserve Sharing Group (RSG) requested contingency reserve delivery from the NWPP RSG.
PACE made an initial request of 2,668 MW at 12:47:00; WACM requested 222 MW at 12:48:30; and Berkshire-Hathaway Energy–MT (BHE-MT) requested 110 MW at 12:46:50.
The NWPP RSG program distributed this request to every remaining NWPP RSG member, which includes most of the WI Balancing Authorities (BA).
At 12:55:26, PACE raised its request to 3,639 MW.
In response to the delivery of contingency reserves, WI frequency recovered to nominal 60.0 Hz at approximately 12:49:42, roughly 6 minutes after the event started.
Entities requesting contingency reserve deliveries continued to modify their requests throughout the event.

System Restoration Restoration Training and System Assessment Large-scale events on the BES that require coordinated restoration are rare.
This makes it difficult to develop and maintain the skills needed in the restoration process.
To reinforce the importance of this crucial task, and to develop and maintain the skills needed, system operators are required to perform yearly training on restoration provided by their RCs.
Most restoration training is built on a full-area blackout scenario.
In this training model, operators focus on executing their entity’s blackstart restoration procedure and coordinating each stage of progress with the RC.
When the system is ready to reconnect with adjacent Transmission Operator (TOP) areas, the RC is responsible for coordinating and approving—or withholding approval for—the interconnection.
During an event such as the one experienced on November 13, system restoration depends heavily on the post-disturbance condition of the remaining interconnection.
This form of restoration, recovering a partially intact but stressed system rather than initiating a full blackstart, is not typically emphasized in training.
As a result, operators must rely on the restoration principles and decision-making skills developed through their training and apply them dynamically to the conditions at hand.
Recommendation An accurate assessment of the condition of the system after a cascading event is needed to implement coordinated restoration.
After the event, entities work with their RCs to determine the extent and condition of the affected area.

This assessment should include information on: • Boundaries of the affected areas • Generation status and availability • Transmission line status • Load status • Voltage and frequency • System operating limits (SOL) exceedances Properly identifying the condition of the area and the resources available will aid in the coordinated restoration after an event.
The area of the power system affected in this event is also characterized by relatively low pockets of load, abundant generation, and long transmission lines that interconnect them.
This configuration can lead to issues controlling system voltages.
As the transmission lines are placed in service, they will initially increase the voltage.
As system load, generation, and voltage control devices are placed in service, they will help to bring the voltage back within its normal operating range.
System operators must plan their restoration to successfully maintain this balance.
In those areas where sections of the power system are split between multiple system operators, communication and coordination become vital to facilitate a smooth and successful restoration process.
Restoration Challenges After the system event, the entities worked toward restoring their systems.
The quality of the restoration during the November 13 event was affected by several issues in the categories of personnel, processes, and tools.
Personnel Among the affected entities, there was a lack of mutual understanding of what occurred, the extent of the outage, and how to proceed forward.
The volume of calls into some of the control centers exceeded the ability of the operators to successfully manage them.
Many of the assessments performed failed to provide the necessary information.

Some entities, not recognizing the extent of the tripping, determined that it was a Balancing Contingency Event (BCE) and worked to recover ACE and Contingency Reserves but did not follow the guidance documented in their restoration plans.
These factors resulted in operational silos with an initial failure to efficiently assess the extent of the outage and collaborate on restoration.
Processes All the entities involved provided their restoration plans through a data request to the review team.
These documents are used to help them plan their response to a system disturbance.
In these documents, one of the primary starting points was assessing their systems to establish the boundaries, impacts, and status.
Absence of initial identification of the full scope and impact of this event initially led to an overall lack of coordination in restoration.
This event affected entities in two RC areas.
It is critical and expected that the RCs would communicate and coordinate the restoration efforts across their area seams.

RCW initially determined the event did not meet the criteria to trigger a restoration plan and contacted PACE in its area asking whether it thought it would be able to recover its Reporting Area Control Error (ACE) 20.
SPP’s initial response was to notify its TOPs through a bridge call that it would work to mitigate numerous N-1 RTCA contingencies and request its entities to hold off on restoration.
SPP set up a bridge call to coordinate restoration at 1416 hrs., with all entities eventually joining the call.
Before this, largely uncoordinated and ineffective restoration efforts had occurred.
Tools Entities were inundated with alarms leading to alarm management issues.
This slowed the identification of causal factors and the extent of the outage.
RCW’s ICCP link for data received from SPP RC for the WACM area went down for 64 minutes, beginning at 1220 hrs.
This outage, combined with the large number of elements affected by the event, caused the state estimator to fail to converge for 32 minutes.
As a result, RCW’s RTCA did not run.
The instantaneous difference between a BA’s actual and scheduled power interchange, plus frequency bias, representing power imbalance.
Several entities’ system displays focused on their local transmission areas but provided a limited view of the interconnection and an overall view of the outage area.
Entities that brought in more of their neighbor’s systems had improved visibility that helped their restoration approach.

BHE identified a difficulty due to its transmission line status (energized/de-energized) being masked by their display design showing lines in service due to breaker status even though they had no voltage or MW power flow.
In all, this limited system visibility added more complexity and confusion to the performance of the assessments and restoration.
Restoration Activities After the system event, SPP’s RTCA showed seven N-1 contingencies with the most severe loading at 160% of that line’s rating.
SPP began a conference bridge with its entities and notified them that coordinated restoration would not begin until the system had been restored to a secure state.
BHE determined its limits of the outage to be the entire northern TOP area (the area of the city of Cheyenne was still energized).
It had open breakers toward its WACM Stegall tie point, and breakers were still closed at the PACE Windstar substation on its ties.
No other 230 kV line breakers in BHE’s internal system had tripped.
SPP declared a transmission emergency for the Wyoming-South Dakota area at 1259 hrs.
This declaration would be released on the morning of November 14.
RCW knew there had been a major generation loss event, but from 1220 hrs. to 1324 hrs. the ICCP links with SPP flatlined with WACM data flatlining also.
This resulted in a loss of visibility into that portion of the system, obscuring RCW’s ability to assess the true magnitude of the event.
With this limited visibility, RCW determined there was no immediate need to initiate its restoration plan.
Its first priorities were to stabilize frequency and recover ACE.
During this time, RCW called PACE and asked whether it would be able to recover.
PACE did not know at this point, stating it was looking “pretty bad.” RCW requested a call within 5 to 10 minutes and stated it may have to shed load.
PACE system operators were focused on recovering their Reporting ACE and initiated a request for contingency reserves to cover the generation loss.
At 1246 hrs., three minutes after the event started, PACE restored the Aeolus–Anticline 500 kV line.

Restoration of this line at the beginning of the restoration process, combined with the lack of area load due to the widespread tripping, contributed to high area voltages that complicated the restoration process.
The Anticline 500 kV North bus reached 587 kV (See Figure 5) with the line returned to service.
The operator inserted reactors at Jim Bridger to help lower the voltage and continued switching to restore the transmission that had tripped.
The operator was unaware of the system connectivity and extent of the impact this restoration was having on neighboring utilities.

600.00 590.00 580.00 570.00 560.00 550.00 540.00 530.00 520.00 510.00 500.00 Figure 5: Anticline 500 kV North bus voltage The TSGT Difficulty substation 230 kV bus voltage reached 266.9 kV exceeding the High Limit 4 level.

This sustained high voltage resulted in TSGT reporting a BES Emergency due to a voltage deviation on a facility equal to or greater than 10% of nominal voltage sustained for greater than or equal to 15 continuous minutes as per the Department of Energy using their Electric Emergency Incident and Disturbance Report.
Later in the event, they also removed their Difficulty substation transformer T1 due to the high system voltages.
Several attempts were made to restore the Badwater substation 230 kV bus beginning at 1300 hrs.
Due to the sustained high system voltage and lack of load, the equipment continued to trip.
PACE continued to restore lines within its system and, at 1300 hrs., completed the 230 kV connection from its Casper substation to its Windstar substation.
This restoration energized the BHE north system from the Windstar interconnection, which was completely de-energized during the initial event.

BHE’s north system was unexpectedly energized by PACE’s action; this resulted in high voltage throughout the BHE system due to all its transmission being intact, no internal generation online, and very low loads due to underfrequency load shed (UFLS) protection operations during the initial trip.
With no notification from PACE that it would be energizing into the BHE system, BHE did not immediately notice its system had been re-energized.

This was due to a combination of its display design, which showed the lines in service based on breaker status, masking their true status, and the overwhelming number of alarms still in the unacknowledged queue from the initial event.
BHE then started to bring on internal combustion turbine generation and loads to help control the high voltage and minimize import energy from Windstar.
It was unable to establish the tie to WACM Stegall due to an excessive phase angle of 100 degrees.
As part of its restoration, PACE worked to provide off-site power to the Dave Johnston substation.
At 13:07:40, the Amasa–Dave Johnston 230 kV line was restored to service, energizing the Dave Johnston 230 kV bus.
Dave Johnston Unit #4, without an electrical interconnection to drive the unit and a trip of the prime mover, had slowed down and reached approximately 3 rpm before re-energization.
With Unit #4 still connected to the now energized bus, the generator started motoring.
The restrained differential relay performed a whole-unit trip (G lockout) at 13:09:50.
The unit experienced substantial damage during this time and remains out of service with no estimated time of restoration.
At 1416 hrs., once SPP had returned its system to a secure state, it initiated a conference bridge for coordinated restoration with all affected parties in both RC areas.

What Went Well Based on discussions with the RCs, coordination between the RCs before and during the event went well.

While it was recognized there were some missed steps during the assessment phase following the event initiation, preceding the trip and even during the restoration phase, the RC-to-RC coordination was positive.
There were several phone calls between the RCs on the morning of the event.

Although there are some areas of improvement for more effective communication, the phone calls revealed great working relationships that have developed over time among the control room operators at RCW, SPP, and PACE.

The RCs worked together to determine the best path forward once the conference call was established, and that coordination created a good culture for the call, which set the tone for the TOPs involved in the restoration.
The RCs coordinated several actions across seams to mitigate the resulting N-1 overloads that were present following the cascade.
There were several N-1 overloads in excess of 150%, and quick action by both RCs returned the system to a secure state quickly.
The TOPs worked together well during this window and coordinated actions across RC seams.
The outcome of these phone calls indicated a very positive, collaborative working relationship between the entities, especially between RCW and SPP, when it comes to mitigating issues around seams.

RCW identified that its EMS alarm system worked very well to show only the most critical alarms to the RC operator (such as frequency/ACE excursions and BES elements out of service) and suppressed non-critical alarms (such as breaker/switch operations).

The RC operators on shift commented that this was very helpful in allowing them to quickly identify the list of BES elements that were out of service without being overwhelmed with switch and breaker alarms.
This significantly improved alarm system was the result of a comprehensive revamp of the alarm philosophy implemented by RCW a few years ago.
RCW noted its wide-area EMS overview display, which showed PACE, WACM, and NWMT systems on one display, was very helpful to the RC operators to quickly assess the scope of the event.

SPP maintained accurate, real-time awareness of system conditions throughout the event, including identification of the Miracle Mile overlap risk, without complete RAS status information from neighboring entities.

SPP's situational awareness applications and real-time engineering support allowed the West RCs to quickly identify the cascade boundary and respond decisively, prioritizing the highest risk single-contingency elements.
The Macomber map and CDAT applications were central to that efficiency.
These applications are available to SPP stakeholders via the Replicated Data Server, giving customers direct access to RC-level system visibility.
SPP commended BHE on its initial actions, its assessment, its speed of response, and accuracy of its decision making.
Throughout the event their staff remained calm and were easy to work with despite the fact their system was affected the most by the event.
BHE noted that the RC bridge call became a turning point once all parties were able to join.
The BHE OEs played a critical role by helping operators identify a major system limitation: specifically, that the entire northern system was being supplied through a single tie.

Its backup power system performed very well and kept its EMS/supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)25 system running with no interruptions, which greatly assisted the restoration.

Entities should use conservative decision-making in verifying any discrepancies between RTCA results.

When addressing N-1 contingencies post-event, RCs should consider whether returning lines to service would resolve some of these contingencies more efficiently and quicker than other methods. o Direct TOPs to restore their systems as much as possible without interconnecting with neighboring TOPs.

Entities should ensure consistent modeling of system parameters such as RAS status.

Entities should examine their quality control procedures for the implementation of new software or changes to existing software to ensure the settings are accurate.

TOPs should examine their systems to identify any single-source data point used to establish equipment status and consider adding additional sources if feasible, e.g., line status from voltage and breaker position.

Appendix A — OPA RCs and TOPs perform various studies to gain insights into their system.
These studies are performed for different periods: long-term, seasonal, near-real time, and real time.
An OPA is a study performed the day before.
These studies provide value by taking in the most accurate load and generation forecasts available combined with expected topology for the upcoming day.
This allows entities to identify challenges in advance, so mitigation plans can be created to account for challenges that may appear in real time.
There are several ways to perform an OPA, a few of which are detailed below.
Next-Day OPA Study PACE’s process for creating a next-day OPA study involves taking a snapshot of the most recent peak load case, including the generation levels during peak load.
Since the next-day OPA case only captures an hour of the operating day, it is limited on which outages are captured and studied.
On November 13, 2025, the outage to the Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line on PACE's system was scheduled to take place at 0800 hrs. and expected to be out of service for about an hour.
Delays in getting personnel on site to perform the switching pushed the outage several hours later than originally scheduled.
The shift resulted in wind generation levels for Wyoming being significantly higher than the levels studied in the OPA.
RCW's OPA includes 24 hours in its next-day OPA study case, which includes forecast generation.

Since the Aeolus–Clover line was scheduled to come out of service at 0800 hrs., the forecast generation levels in the next-day OPA were low enough to not cause any post contingent overloads or voltage issues, therefore, there was no mitigation plan, including RAS action, developed for this outage.
SPP creates an OPA case based on the most recent peak load case, capturing generation levels at the time of the snapshot.

SPP had concerns with generation levels with the concurrent outages of the Miracle Mile bus and the Aeolus–Clover line, but those concerns and generation limitations were not explicitly coordinated with RCW or PACE.

Conclusion: With the Aeolus–Clover outage being delayed from 0800 to 1200 hrs., and the wind generation forecasts being 1,000+ MWs lower at 0800 than at 1200 hrs., the OPA did not reveal any potential issues regarding the Aeolus–Clover outage any of the three entities.
The concern identified in the OPA was directed toward the concurrent outages of the Miracle Mile bus and the Aeolus–Clover line.

Restoration This event affected facilities in two RC areas and five TOP areas.
After a system event like this, power system restoration depends on the initial condition of the rest of the interconnection.
The affected TOPs and RCs implement their restoration plans to coordinate the recovery process.
These restoration plans begin with an initial assessment by the RCs and TOPs to determine the extent and condition of the affected area(s).
Once this assessment is complete, the operators will begin restoring their TOP area.
Communication and coordination with the RCs and neighboring TOPs at the areas where they interconnect is critical to prevent incorrect operations from delaying the restoration process.

its system again, tripping the NE Wyoming and BHE area.

reference_summary: On November 13, 2025, at 1243 hrs.1, the northeast region of the Western Interconnection (WI) experienced a significant system disturbance that resulted in cascading line outages and affected approximately 250,000 customers, lasting up to 9.5 hours in some areas. This disturbance affected parts of several states, including Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Nebraska, and Black Hills Energy (BHE) experienced a complete blackout of its northern system (western South Dakota and northeast Wyoming). The Montana–Alberta Tie Line (MATL) — WECC Path 83 — also tripped during this event. The affected region was situated between the boundaries of the RC West (RCW) and the SPP West (SPP) Reliability Coordinator (RC) areas. The disturbance was triggered by a planned outage of a single 500 kV transmission line, but multiple factors exacerbated the situation, contributing to the widespread outage. See Figure 2, page 9. The line that was scheduled to be out of service was the PacifiCorp East (PACE) Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line. This line, along with the Aeolus–Anticline 500 kV line, transfers large amounts of wind and thermal generation in this region to load centers across the interconnection. The Aeolus lines require close monitoring, and outages may necessitate limiting wind generation in the area. To ensure reliable operation, PACE implemented a Remedial Action Scheme (RAS)2 that automatically trips wind generation for outages of the 500 kV Aeolus lines, preventing broader system disturbances. The outage of this line was planned for November 13 at 0800 in accordance with established PACE and RCW processes. On the morning of the planned outage, PACE determined that field personnel would not be available to perform the required switching until noon. RCW and SPP had previously coordinated and agreed that the outage of the Western Area Power Administration-Rocky Mountain Region (WACM) and the outage of the Miracle Mile-Alcova west 115 kV line would not be allowed to overlap. During this delay, RCW and SPP worked with WACM and PACE to determine what would be needed if the outages were overlapped. As the morning passed, wind generation increased in the area, which increased the amount of energy flowing across the two Aeolus 500 kV lines. As the time for the planned outage approached, PACE, adhering to its operating practices, modified the Aeolus RAS by raising the arming setpoint to ensure the RAS would not inadvertently operate during switching. PACE monitored its Real-time Contingency Analysis (RTCA)3 for system operating violations and found none; however, PACE was unaware that RTCA alarming functions had not been enabled and that incorrect parameters were masking the results. All times in this report are given in Mountain Standard Time (MST). A scheme designed to detect predetermined System conditions and automatically take corrective actions that may include adjusting or tripping generation (MW and Mvar), tripping load, or reconfiguring a System(s). Real-Time Contingency Analysis (RTCA) evaluates system conditions, such as load, generation, and transmission outages, using real-time data to assess both current and future operating conditions. It continuously simulates equipment failures or network changes and allows operators to prepare for, or automatically trigger, corrective actions (e.g., re-dispatching, switching) to mitigate risks. With no violations identified, PACE removed the Aeolus–Clover line from service, operating the system in an unidentified Normal-1 (N-1)4 insecure state, which resulted in a cascading outage. This cascading was due to a shift of flows onto the Aeolus–Anticline line, which caused the local voltage to collapse to 138 kV (~0.28 pu)5. As designed, protective relaying tripped the Aeolus–Anticline line within 0.4 seconds of the initial loss of the Aeolus–Clover line. Subsequently, power flow rapidly redistributed throughout the northeast portion of the WI. While most of the WI remained functional, the disturbance culminated in the loss of more than 4,800 MW of generation from coal, natural gas, photovoltaic, and wind resources. Within 6 seconds, an electrical island formed and collapsed, causing widespread effects across that portion of the interconnection. The Aeolus RAS did not trip any generation because its setpoint had been raised before switching. The resulting generation-load imbalance caused the WI frequency to drop to 59.758 Hz before recovering to 60 Hz within approximately 6 minutes, and underfrequency load shedding was activated in the northeastern region before the island collapse. In terms of system voltages, 500 kV voltages ranged from a nominal value of approximately 520 kV (~1.0 pu) to lows of 138 kV (~0.28 pu) during the initiating part of the event and before system separation. Due to the rapid progression of this event, no manual corrective actions were able to be taken during the trip. As a result of this cascading outage, customers in PACE, BHE, Tri-State G&T (TSGT), and WACM lost power for hours, with some industrial load customers remaining out of service until the following day. 1. PACE lost 411.1 MW of firm load, affecting approximately 54,000 customers. 2. WACM lost 709 MW of firm load in its Balancing Authority Area (BAA), affecting approximately 47,000 sub-BA customers. It also included: o 538 MW of firm load in BHE, affecting approximately 154,000 customers o 6.64 MW of firm load in TSGT, affecting approximately 1,900 customers Although wind generation was substantial at the time of the event, it was not identified as a contributing factor. Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been implicated in other disturbance events6. The IBRs in eastern Wyoming tripped appropriately for the over-/under-voltage and frequency conditions of the event. After thorough analysis, it was found that all IBR protection and control settings operated as designed. In addition, IBRs supported a faster frequency recovery across the interconnection, driven largely by battery energy storage systems, while wind generation provided readily available capacity during system restoration. A secure state is a condition where the power system is operating within all design constraints and can withstand the unexpected failure of any single key component — such as a transmission line, transformer, or generator — without violating security limits or causing a service interruption. Per unit (pu) converts actual volts to a dimensionless fraction, where 1.0 pu typically represents the nominal or rated voltage. Inverter-Based Resource Disturbances in the Western Interconnection ; October 2025 After the event, the affected entities began their respective restoration processes. Restoration power was available to all entities from either their own systems or neighboring systems. Restoration efforts included mitigation of multiple N-1 contingencies, difficulties caused by high voltage levels, large phase angles, and inadequate communication, which resulted in instances of equipment energization between TOPs across the RC seams with no prior communication. The restoration of most facilities and loads took approximately 9 hours. PACE completed restoration of its last loads within 9.5 hours. BHE successfully restored most of its customers within 7 hours, although some industrial loads were not restored until the next day. TSGT and WACM completed their load restorations within 8.5 hours. PACE had most of its generation available within 8 hours. One thermal generation facility took over four days to recover, with one additional generator remaining out of service due to significant damage that occurred during restoration. See Figure 4, page 8. Key Contributors Key contributors were identified through the disturbance review and categorized into three primary groups: personnel, processes, and tools. Personnel • There was inadequate mutual understanding between RCs and Transmission Operators (TOP) when communicating and sharing details of the planned outage (e.g., RTCA results, final switching approval, RAS status). Processes • Processes in place for some entities were inadequate to manage seams across TOP and RC areas, (e.g., incomplete modeling of neighboring systems in operational planning analysis (OPA)7, RTCA models), along with inadequate sharing of real-time operational data, such as RAS status and related information. • Persistent issues with the RTCA were never fully resolved; workarounds were used to allow studies to run. This led operators to lose confidence in the RTCA’s results for the affected part of the interconnection, and it delayed action while studies were being run. Tools • Some TOPs mainly rely on a single analysis tool and its model without the capacity to validate results across offline and online study tools. • RCs and TOPs made different assumptions when modeling the Aeolus RAS in each of their RTCA models. An evaluation of projected system conditions to assess anticipated (pre-contingency) and potential (post contingency) conditions for next day operations. • RTCA for one entity used inaccurate modeling parameters, such as operating limits and generating resource reactive capability, and had disabled alarming functions for low voltages. There was also a lack of consistency with generator testing parameters.
title: November 13 Wyoming Disturbance Report

candidate_sentences.text: IBRs continue to trip for non-consequential faults on the Bulk Power System (BPS).
The four events in this report that exceeded the threshold of a NERC Categorized 1i event due to loss of more than 500 MW of IBR generation show that there is still a need for Reliability Standards.
This section describes the initiating fault and gives an overview of the affected IBR facilities for each of the four disturbances analyzed.

Predisturbance Operating Conditions Figure 1 shows solar PV power profiles for the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) each day that disturbances occurred, and Figure 2 shows the solar PV power profile for PacifiCorp East (PACE) for that disturbance.
Table 2 shows predisturbance operating conditions for each fault.

BPSconnected IBR (wind, solar PV, and BESS) output ranged from 30% to 81% of the CAISO internal net demand and 38% of the PACE internal net demand at the time of each fault, with solar PV providing less than 1% for the May 20 event due to the event time.

These predisturbance operating conditions illustrate the significant amount of IBR capacity in the CAISO and PACE footprints and highlight the importance of ensuring that all BPS-connected IBRs are operating in a manner that supports reliable operation of the BPS.
Figure 1: CAISO total solar PV profiles for each day events occurred.
￼ Figure 2: PACE total solar PV profile for the day event occurred.

Table 2: Predisturbance Operating Conditions Value % Value % Value % Value % Description of Disturbances March 25, 2024 “Vincent Disturbance”: At 14:55:52, the Vincent 500kV South bus, along with 3AA and 4AA banks, relayed during restoration of a power circuit breaker after scheduled maintenance at Vincent.
CAISO observed a 1,046 MW reduction in solar PV and wind resources across the area.
CAISO identified 28 facilities that reduced output due to the fault.
Figure 3: Fault clearing for March 25 disturbance.
May 12, 2024 “Red Butte Disturbance”: At 07:06 the Hickory-Red Butte 345kV line relayed out on a phase-to-phase fault.
PACE observed a 532 MW reduction in solar PV resources across the area.
PACE identified eight solar PV facilities that reduced output due to the fault.
Figure 4: Fault clearing for May 12 disturbance.
May 20, 2024 “Windhub Disturbance”: At 21:10:04, the Windhub 500/230 kV 3AA transformer bank tripped on differential protection when a riser lead became separated.
CAISO observed a 698 MW reduction in solar PV, wind, and BESS resources.
Due to the event time, the majority loss was wind and BESS for this incident.
CAISO identified 22 facilities that reduced output due to the fault.
Figure 5: Fault clearing for May 20 disturbance.
June 15, 2024 “Post Fire Disturbance”: At 15:06:40, the Post fire burning near the Midway-Vincent corridor resulted in the trip of the Midway-Vincent #1 500kV line.
CAISO observed a 934 MW reduction in solar PV, wind, and BESS resources.
At 15:07, the Midway-Vincent #2 500kV line also tripped.
The lines remained out of service until the fire burned clear of the corridor.
CAISO identified 37 facilities that reduced output due to the fault.

Figure 6: Fault clearing for June 15 disturbance Findings and Recommended Actions • Finding: In one of the events, it was found that IBRs that had made changes in settings to improve their performance due to faults, had reverted to the previous settings during a firmware update.
These previous settings allowed tripping of the facility due to the fault during this event.
Appendix A: Industry Efforts Industry is working to address this risk in a variety of ways.
FERC On October 30, 2023, FERC issued Order No.
901 Reliability Standards to Address Inverter-Based Resources, directing NERC to develop new or modified standards to address reliability gaps identified through the performance of IBRs since 2016.
The four areas identified to be addressed are: • IBR Data Sharing, • IBR Model Validation, • IBR Planning and Operational studies, and • IBR Performance Requirements.
NERC In response to FERC Order 901, NERC developed an implementation plan composed of four milestones: 1.
Standards development and filing to address performance requirements and post-performance requirements and post-performance validations for Registered IBRs, 3.
Development and filing of Reliability Standards to address data sharing and model validation for all IBRs, and 4.
Development and filing of Reliability Standards to address use of performance data in Operational and Planning studies.
At the time of this report, Milestones 1 and 2 have been completed.

As part of the Milestone 2, on February 20, 2025, FERC approved PRC-028-1, Disturbance Monitoring and Reporting Requirements for Inverter-Based Resources and PRC-030-1, Unexpected Inverter-Based Resource Event Mitigation and on July 25, 2025 FERC approved PRC-029-1, Frequency and Voltage Ride-through Requirements for Inverter-Based Resources.
This also includes the addition of a definition for the term “Ride-through” to the Glossary of Terms Used in NERC Reliability Standards.
Milestone 3 is underway, with a projected due date for the standards of November 4, 2025.

This effort is working toward updates to NERC Standards: • MOD-026, Verification of Models and Data for Generator Excitation Control System or Plant Volt/Var Control Functions. • MOD-032, Data for Power System Modeling and Analysis. • MOD-033, Steady-State and Dynamic System Model Validation.
Milestone 4 has a projected due date of November 4, 2026, with Standard Authorization Requests expected to be published around August.
WECC On March 14, 2023, NERC issued a Level 2 NERC Alert on IBR performance issues.
As part of this alert, NERC asked entities whether the inverter voltage and frequency protection settings were based on the maximum capability of the equipment.

In its November 2023 Inverter-Based Resource Performance Issues Report, NERC reported that results show less than one-third of the inverter settings reported are set based on equipment capability, meaning there is significant underused ride-through capability across the BPS.

NERC also reported that this finding raises concerns regarding ride-through performance, the provision of essential reliability services, and BPS reliability, especially now, as the grid is undergoing retirements of substantial amounts of synchronous machines.

In the June 2022 Odessa Disturbance Report, NERC reported that for some of the causes of tripping “The inverter manufacturer stated that they plan to only make changes to facilities that request the update and do not have any plans to proactively update or mitigate this risk on their end.” In the report, NERC strongly recommended that all GOs with these inverters seek immediate updates (when available) to their in-service inverters to mitigate the possibility of unexpected and abnormal tripping for BPS faults.

WECC, using the Level 2 NERC alert data and disturbance report recommendation, identified 77 IBR facilities within the Western Interconnection that indicated their IBR inverters were not optimized for performance based on equipment limitations.

Building on previous outreach efforts, in April 2024, WECC began contacting these facilities requesting they voluntarily work with their OEM for the equipment and adjust the inverter settings using the maximum capability of the equipment.
By October 2024, WECC had received responses from 87% of the identified facilities.
CAISO CAISO IBR Operational Performance Investigations Technical requirements for IBRs are set out in the ISO’s Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (LGIA).

These changes were made due to several factors, including: • Between the months of August and February 2017 there were eight transmission system faults in ISO’s BA that resulted in the unanticipated loss of approximately 1200 MW of inverter-based generation per event. • After seeking to enlist support for adding requirements to NERC Standards, the ISO conducted a stakeholder process and revised its pro forma LGIA and SGIA agreements to include specific technical IBR requirements.
FERC adopted the changes in April 2019.
The requirements were performance-based and set specific conditions for all non-synchronous generation sources interconnecting to the ISO transmission system.

The ISO monitors and investigates non-compliance with the performance requirements The ISO follows a process similar to this: Figure 7: Desktop procedure overview The ISO follows these review steps: 1.
Our staff uses CAISO’s operating logs, frequency deviations, and SCADA to monitor the CAISO total generation curve.

If we observe a total generation reduction of greater than 500 MW that is predicated by a transmission event, ISO staff will analyze the event to determine whether there was an aggregate reduction of 250 MW or more of IBR resources.
Operations staff then requests data from the affected TOP, including PMU, SCADA, and any associated relay records.
Resources with reductions of 2 MW or more are identified, but the threshold for further analysis is 10 MW.
Our transmission team will review the data and use contact information to issue an IBR data request.

We also review past event analysis to determine whether the facility has been involved in previous events, is currently working to mitigate any improper operations, or whether it is a legacy facility not subject to revised LGIA requirements.
After reviewing the submitted data, we will coordinate with the associated generator to review the facility response.
This meeting will be used to develop action items and next steps to correct or mitigate operational concerns or improper inverter response.

Members of our team also request data from the affected TOP, including PMU, SCADA, and any relay records to assist in the investigation including: • Electrical quantities for the total plant at POI and inverter-level signals. • DFR or protective relaying data, if available, in Comtrade format. • Summary of inverters that tripped or entered momentary cessation including the associated fault codes. • Detailed accounting of the duration of cessation or fault for all affected inverters. • Plant single lines identifying affected inverters. • Power Plant Controller (PPC) type and response/control data during the event. • Facility information including inverter manufacturer and model. • Inverter control settings. • Most current EMT and Planning Study Model.
If an escalation is required to enforce the operational requirements of the LGIA, our staff will issue a contract breach letter.
All mitigation plans, meeting minutes, analysis, and associated documentation for each event will be archived by the CAISO.

LGIA Appendix HH: “An Asynchronous Generating Facility shall remain online for the voltage disturbance caused by any fault on the transmission grid … having a duration equal to the lesser of the normal three-phase fault clearing time (4–9 cycles) or one-hundred fifty (150) milliseconds.” Sample Data:
Figure 8: Sample reduction data An example of the findings could look like this: • Faulted units: DC overvoltage, over/under frequency, AC overcurrent, Module Fault, Unbalanced Voltage AC or DC.
Resolutions: • Typical resolutions involve firmware upgrades, setting changes, or both.

Challenges: • More events that are not predicated by a transmission event due to better tools and operator training/familiarity such as oscillations and loss of generation. • Date granularity and synchronization of data records are an ongoing challenge to accurately diagnosing events.

reference_summary: NERC and Regional Entities continue to analyze disturbances involving widespread reduction of inverter-based resources (IBR) to identify any systemic reliability issues to support affected facilities as they develop mitigating measures, and to share key findings and recommendations with industry for increased awareness and action. The events identified in this report confirm that the ongoing widespread reduction of IBR resources is a notable reliability risk to the bulk power system (BPS). This report contains four BPS disturbances involving widespread reduction of IBR output that occurred in WECC’s footprint between March and June 2024. Each disturbance was categorized as a Category 1i event per the NERC Event Analysis Process and involved widespread reduction of active power output from solar photovoltaic (PV), wind, and battery energy storage system (BESS) / hybrid resources in the entity area (specifically in areas of high penetrations of solar PV and wind resources). One of the events occurred at a time when most of the solar PV resources were not producing power and involved generation loss at both wind and BESS IBR facilities. All initiating faults were normally cleared with proper protection system operation. These four disturbances further show the need to ensure all BPS-connected IBRs operate reliably to support the BPS. Table 1 is an overview of the four disturbances analyzed by NERC and WECC. Table 1: Overview of Disturbances Disturbance Initiating Fault Event Description of Resource Loss* March 25, 2024 Phase-to-Ground Fault on 500 kV Loss of 1046 MW of solar PV and “Vincent Disturbance” bus wind resources (28 units) May 12, 2024 Phase-to-Ground Fault on 345 kV Loss of 532 MW of solar PV “Red Butte Disturbance” Line resources (8 units) May 20, 2024 Differential trip on 500/220 kV Loss of 698 MW of solar PV, wind, “Windhub Disturbance” Transformer and BESS resources (22 units) June 15, 2024 Phase-to-Phase Fault on 500 kV Loss of 934 MW of solar PV, wind, “Post fire Disturbance” Line and BESS resources (37 units) Recommended Actions Based on the findings of this work, WECC recommends the following actions for entities to take. 1. During updates to the firmware or software of IBR control equipment, IBR owners/operators should understand what changes are being made and why. All changes should be approved by the owners/operators. 2. Transmission Service Providers may consider what changes, if any, are required in their interconnection agreements to establish an appropriate framework to ensure that IBR-based generation resources perform safely and reliably while interconnected to the BES. 3. IBR owners/operators should identify the user-level inverter grid protection settings for their equipment and adjust these settings utilizing the maximum capability of the equipment. IBR owners/operators should work with the OEM for their equipment to adjust the OEM inverter settings utilizing the maximum capability of the equipment. Making these changes will allow your equipment to better support the reliability of the BES.
title: Inverter-based Resource Disturbances in the Western Interconnection

candidate_sentences.text: This 2022 California Battery Energy Storage System Disturbances report documents the key findings and recommendations from analyzing the abnormal loss of BESS resources that occurred in Southern California on March 9 and April 6, 2022.
This chapter provides details regarding the initiating event, pre-disturbance conditions, overview of disturbances involving BESS, and additional relevant details.
Chapter 2 provides the key findings and establishes the basis for the recommendations.
Appendix A provides a detailed analysis of the affected BESS facilities.
Appendix B provides brief summaries of the affected facilities that are not BESS.
This report focuses solely on the performance and causes of abnormal power reduction.
Description of Analysis Process CAISO identified the events on March 9, 2022, and April 6, 2022, by observing the reduction of power outputs across multiple BESS and solar PV facilities.
The events met the criteria for Category 1a and 1i event, respectively, per the NERC Event Analysis Program based on the total MW losses and number of facilities outaged.
NERC and WECC agreed to develop a disturbance report to share the key findings and recommendations from the analysis with industry.

NERC and WECC decided to focus specifically on BESS due to the unique opportunity of visibility because the first disturbance occurred after sunset (exclusively BESS, no solar) and the same facilities participated in both disturbances.
CAISO independently solicited requests for information to affected entities and also held follow-up calls with those entities to gain any additional information needed to perform root cause analysis.
NERC and WECC collaborated with CAISO and prepared this report based on the information provided by CAISO.
Pre-disturbance Operating Conditions The March disturbance occurred at 18:03:20 Pacific time after the sun had set.
The April disturbance occurred at 15:06:05 Pacific time when the solar PV facilities were still producing power.
Most of the affected BESS facilities were located in the vicinity of solar PV facilities.
While solar PV facilities were involved in the April event, this report specifically focuses on the BESS facilities.
Table 1.1 shows the generation mix prior to the disturbances.

Table 1.1: Pre-disturbance Resource Mix Resource Type March 9 April 6 BESS 769.4 212.1 Overview of Disturbances involving BESS This report covers the following two events that occurred in March and April of 2022: • March 9, 2022: At 18:03:20 Pacific time, a generator bus was faulted when a generator circuit breaker had an internal failure at a natural-gas-fired, simple-cycle facility in Riverside County, California, causing a C-phaseto-ground fault on the 220 kV system.
Generator units relayed, disconnecting the natural gas generators that were carrying 694 MW.
The fault was cleared in approximately 4.5 cycles.
In addition, inverter-based resources from many different facilities also unexpectedly reduced 408 MW, 124 MW of which is attributed to BESS.
The fault therefore resulted in a total loss of 1,102 MW of generation, and system frequency dropped
CAISO, the Balancing Authority, raised regulating unit output to assist in the recovery of the frequency and ACE.
The time from the event start to the frequency nadir was measured at around 12 seconds.
System frequency returned to normal in three minutes. • April 6, 2022: At 15:06:05 Pacific time, a B-phase-to-ground fault occurred on a 220 kV bus at a new BESS plant that was undergoing testing.
The fault was cleared in approximately four cycles.
The normally cleared fault resulted in an unexpected reduction of 498 MW from multiple inverter-based resources.
The loss of generation caused the system frequency to fall from around 60.014 Hz to 59.924 Hz.
The time from the event start to the frequency nadir was around seven seconds.
The CAISO Balancing Authority raised regulating unit output to assist in recovery of the frequency and ACE.
System frequency returned to normal in one and half minutes.
In both events, the faults occurred in the Southern California area within the CAISO footprint.
Multiple BESS and solar PV facilities were identified as exhibiting unreliable performance.
All affected facilities are within or near the Southern California area (see Figure 1.1 and Figure 1.2).
Figure 1.3 and Figure 1.4 show the reduction in solar PV and BESS resources reported by Southern California Edison (SCE) Operations for each disturbance.
Figure 1.5 shows the Western Interconnection frequency from PMU data at nearby 500 kV substation for both disturbances.

Chapter 2: Detailed Findings from Disturbance Analysis This chapter describes the key findings from this analysis, including corrective actions taken by CAISO and GOs.
Refer to Appendix A for details regarding each affected facility.
Causes of BESS Abnormal Power Reduction The causes of abnormal active power reduction for each BESS or hybrid facility are listed in Table 2.1.
The facilities saw multiple inverters trip due to multiple causes, making it difficult to break down active power reductions by fault codes.

Table 2.1: Causes of BESS Abnormal Power Reduction Cause of Reduction Plant A Plant B Plant C Plant D Original Equipment Power Electronics Power Electronics Power Electronics Power Electronics Manufacturer March April March April March April March April AC Overcurrent X X X AC Overvoltage X Inconclusive DC Bus Voltage X due to poor Unbalance Not metering Involved data to Unbalanced AC Current X X X X support GOs claims DC Overvoltage X X Half Bus DC Vmax X Unknown/Misc.
X X X X * Not available due to data quality and availability issues detailed in Appendix A.
Previously Reported Causes of Tripping Most affected facilities experienced the following causes of inverter tripping that have already been extensively covered in previous disturbance reports.

Therefore, technical details regarding them are omitted in this report: • Inverter instantaneous ac overcurrent • Inverter instantaneous ac overvoltage tripping • Inverter dc voltage unbalance tripping Other causes of tripping not identified in previous disturbance reports are detailed in the following sections.
Inverter Unbalanced AC Current Tripping This is the most common cause of tripping observed in both disturbances.
The inverter module can trip when an unbalance has been detected in the module output currents that are above a programmed threshold and remains for longer than a programmed time delay.

Chapter 2: Detailed Findings from Disturbance Analysis Inverter DC Bus Overvoltage Inverter dc bus overvoltage tripping was observed in two facilities: one while discharging and another while charging.
Inverter Half DC Bus Overvoltage This protection is triggered when an inverter module continues to experience unstable dc bus voltage despite being stopped on dc bus overvoltage fault.
Data Quality None of the facilities involved met CAISO’s requirement of 10 ms data recording resolution.
No inverter-level oscillography data was available from any of the facilities involved because they did not have the required fast logging enabled.
CAISO reported that these deficiencies have been corrected.

Miscoding Inverter Faults While one facility had legacy inverters that utilize momentary cessation, GOs of other affected facilities have miscoded inverter tripping lasting tens of seconds as momentary cessation.
Momentary cessation is a controlled behavior during certain grid conditions and is vastly different from an inverter tripping inadvertently and reconnecting after a short time.
One facility only reported high level inverter fault codes, which do not provide any useful insights.
The inverters involved in these events are made up of multiple modules, and inverters can experience loss of all or some of the modules (partial trip).
The actual trip mechanism, as part of self-protection design, occurs within the modules and thus the module fault codes are more meaningful.
NERC recommends all GOs log and report module fault codes.

Mitigations through CAISO Enforcement of Interconnection Agreement Based on the findings from the two BESS events, CAISO identified that the affected facilities did not meet the performance-related requirements of the Generator Interconnection Agreement (GIA).
8 Subsequently, CAISO issued notice of breach letters to affected GOs advising that the terms and conditions of Appendix H of the LGIA are not being met by their facilities.
The notice highlighted the provisions related to the voltage ride-through and minimum transient data recording requirements.

The letter required GOs of affected BESS facilities to develop and implement mitigation plans to eliminate the unexpected causes of tripping and make changes to recording capabilities to meet the interconnection agreement requirements.
The following summarizes the corrective actions taken by CAISO and GOs: • CAISO reported that all but one facility has been enhanced with inverter software upgrades.
The software upgrades increased the threshold for dc bus unbalance tripping and implemented faster activation of stronger dc balancing and faster activation of low voltage ride-through mode.
CAISO reviewed evidence of the effectiveness of the mitigation plans provided by the GOs working with the inverter manufacturer.

Evidence includes the lab test results from the inverter manufacturer that showed the performance of the inverter before and after the software upgrade. • These enhanced facilities performed better during an event in February 2023 that involved an unbalanced grid fault.

This suggests some evidence of the efficacy of the changes implemented post 2022 events. • CAISO updated technical requirements of their pro forma LGIA, requiring the plant controller to be coordinated with the inverters so that the plant controller will not restrict inverter reconnection following the clearance of a low voltage transient.

Plant C Plant C is a 250 MW facility connected to the 230 kV network that went into commercial operation in June 2021.
The plant reduced output by 73 MW during the event (see Figure A.2).
The plant consists of a total of 88 inverters.
Of these, 27 inverters experienced instantaneous ac overcurrent tripping, and 35 inverters experienced unbalanced ac current tripping.

Inverter logs show 12 inverters tripped and 1 inverter was already off-line before the event.

Table A.2 provides an overview of the BESS facilities involved in the April event followed by additional details for each specific facility.
